sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
Self-powered devices are becoming highly ubiquitous and receiving increasing interest as they dispense the need for replacement of chemical batteries. The abundant renewable energy resources such as solar, wind, thermal, pressure, human power, vibrations, etc. are generally underutilized for energy harvesting. One of the most common and unused energy resources is vibration. The vibration energy harvesting follows three mechanisms: electromagnetic (Chiu et al., 2012), electrostatic (Liu et al., 2012) and piezoelectric (Hu et al., 2007a). Among these, piezoelectric energy harvesting is of great importance because of its low cost, easy integration, resilience, maximum conversion efficiency and ability to withstand in many challenging environments (Kirubaveni et al., 2015). Piezoelectric materials with high piezoelectric coefficient and electromechanical coupling factor make them suitable for energy harvesting applications. The geometry of a piezoelectric cantilever beam is found to have a greater impact on its conversion efficiency (Savarimuthu et al., 2017). Hence, alternative cantilever beam geometries are of much interest for considerable reduction in resonant frequency with maximum output power. In literature, several cantilever geometries such as corrugation shape (Hongping et al., 2008), zigzag structure (Karami and Inman, 2012) and cruciform shape (Tsuruta et al., 2016) are reported to improve the realized output power. A brief analytical comparison is made between a rectangular cantilever and a triangular cantilever. A triangular cantilever has a higher strain and deflection for a given load resistance. The strain distributions of rectangular, trapezoidal and triangular piezoelectric cantilevers were also analyzed. Simulation and experimental results demonstrated the presence of improved strain distribution in the triangular cantilever under identical conditions and ability to generate more voltage than the counterparts. The strain in a trapezoidal cantilever is more evenly distributed throughout the beam as compared to a rectangular cantilever, which contains a non-uniform strain distribution, and the observed peak normalized power densities are at 2.19 and $4 . 0 5 ~ \mu \mathrm { W } / \mathrm { m m } ^ { 3 }$ for the rectangular and triangular beams, respectively (Ooi et al., 2016). Experiments were carried out with a triangular-shaped and rectangular-shaped piezoelectric vibration energy harvester (PVEH), and it was resolved from the consequences that the triangular-shaped cantilevers were more effectual than rectangular-shaped cantilevers in terms of curvature homogeneity, tolerable excitation amplitude and maximum output power (Goldschimdtboeing and Woias, 2008). The spiral-shaped piezoelectric bimorph harvester with a DC-DC converter and a parallel synchronized switch harvesting on inductor with a harvesting structure can improve the charging efficiency of the battery greatly at a resonant frequency of $5 0 \mathrm { H z }$ (Hu et al., 2007b). Uniform strain distribution can be achieved by changing the top view of the piezoelectric beam. It is also proved that for the same volume of PZT, a trapezoidal cantilever can generate more than twice the energy of a rectangular beam (Park et al., 2010).The efficiency of the energy harvester is improved using piezoelectric stack design and bistable mechanism. By optimizing the shape of the energy harvester, the output power is improved. The trapezoidal geometry improves the output power by 30 per cent per unit volume because of the evenly distributed strain (Benasciutti et al., 2010; Baker et al., 2005). Trapezoidal beam and circularly filleted beam are proposed, simulated and fabricated to enhance the tolerance by reducing the stress level in the material by 60 per cent (Defosseux et al., 2010).

Low frequency piezoelectric energy harvesters are designed by considering linear and quadratic shape variations which maximize the energy output from the harvester. Furthermore, it is inferred that the fundamental natural frequency and mode shape are strongly affected by the beam shape variations (Ben Ayed et al., 2014). An arc and zigzag cantilever using finite element method is proposed. The arc-based cantilever provides 25 per cent frequency reduction, whereas the zigzag design showed only 40 per cent reduction (Apo et al., 2013). A characteristic zigzag shaped beam is compared with flex and elephant beam shapes. From analytical, finite element modeling and experimental measurements, it is found that the elephant harvester has large effective beam tip and low volume with significant power enhancement (Sharpes et al., 2015). A trapezoidal piezoelectric harvester is designed for a specific machine tool application and tested for robustness and longevity. The design focused on resonant performance and distributed strain concentrations at a given acceleration (Reilly et al., 2011). Investigation of the dependency of the generated power and resonant frequency on device dimensions and geometries has been done for standardizing comparisons. In this paper, cantilevers in rectangle, triangle and trapezoid shapes are modeled, and their performances are analyzed using simulation and experimentation. In a study by Savarimuthu et al. (2017), power conditioning circuits are analyzed to improve the performance of piezoelectric energy harvester. However, the authors have tested the performance of the harvester by using commercially available piezo device. Hence, this manuscript presents new cantilever architectures for energy harvesting from ambient vibrations.

The main focus of this paper is a comparison of the performance of various geometric shapes of monomorph cantilever beams. It is organized as follows: Section II focuses on the design of energy harvester under analysis. The mathematical modeling of PVEH in different geometries is addressed in Section III. The performance comparison of harvesters based on finite element method analysis and experimental results are reviewed in Section IV. Section V describes the integration of power conditioning circuit with optimum harvester to power up the C-mote node. Finally, from the discussed results, conclusions are drawn in section VI.

sections.heading: 2. Energy harvester description
sections.text:
Among the different available configurations, cantilever beam configurations are widely used as they exhibit lower resonant frequencies compared to other configurations, such as diaphragm and bridge (Roundy et al., 2005), and maximum power is harvested (Savarimuthu et al., 2017). The proposed PVEH is constructed using a cantilever beam with one end fixed using a rigid support and the other end is left free. The harvester consists of two layers, namely, the top and bottom layers. The top layer is made using PZT 5H having a high electromechanical coupling coefficient and maximum energy harvesting capability. The bottom layer is constructed using aluminum because of its relative softness, durability, lightweight and ductility (Street and Alexander, 1994). The properties of the material under consideration are listed in Table I.

The dimensions and the shape of the cantilever have an effect on the output power, as the strain induced in each case is unique. To analyze the effect of shape on the harvester's performance, cantilever beams in rectangular, triangular and trapezoidal shapes are considered and analyzed.

sections.heading: 3. Mathematical modeling
sections.text:
Mathematical modeling of the PVEH is performed by splitting the cantilever into three sections by using the Euler-Bernoulli beam theory. Sections I and III comprise the substrate layer (aluminum), and Section II has both substrate and piezo layer (aluminum and PZT 5H). A sectional view of the proposed trapezoidal cantilever is shown in Figure 1. The performance of energy harvesters in different geometries is analyzed by observing their frequency and power analysis. sections.text:

The comparative analysis is tabulated in Figure 2. The main goal considered in designing a PVEH is the achievement of maximum output power at low resonant frequency. It is imperative for the cantilevers to be excited at the first natural frequency where they undergo maximum deformation to produce the maximum electrical power from the piezoelectric element attached to the vibrating cantilevers. The first resonant mode shape of the harvester with corresponding eigenfrequency analysis is shown in Figure 2. From the mode shapes in Figure 2, the eigenfrequencies of the cantilever are observed to be 15.198, 30.136 and $2 2 . 7 8 5 \ : \mathrm { H z }$ for rectangular, triangular and trapezoidal cantilever, respectively. The rectangular cantilever provides lower resonant frequency in comparison with other alternate cantilevers. The increase in eigenfrequency is due to the removal of material at the free end. The mass of the cantilever is inversely proportional to the square of the eigenfrequency. The mass of the triangular and trapezoidal cantilever is smaller than the rectangular cantilever, which exhibits higher eigen frequency. ![](images/ea0b55cf97c33b407a01afd5e00e1c5f709fcb6114ee98df6a7ff6aed395061a.jpg) Figure 2 Comparative analysis using FEA A uniform strain distribution is observed while changing the shape of the cantilever, which therefore exhibits maximum stress of $2 . 8 4 \times 1 0 ^ { 7 } \mathrm { \ m P a }$ The maximum stress generated in the proposed trapezoidal cantilever is observed as lower than the fracture stress of aluminum $( 4 8 3 \times 1 0 ^ { 9 } \mathrm { { m P a } ) }$ ; therefore, the design can withstand the large force and hence possess maximum tolerable amplitude.

sections.heading: 4.2.1 Fabrication
sections.text:
With a view to observe the effect of cantilever shape over the resonant frequency and output voltage, aluminum beams with different geometries of the same volume are fabricated and analyzed. The aluminum beam is fabricated using the wire cut electric discharge machining process. Initially, the schematic of the aluminum beam is designed in AutoCAD with dimensions, which are fed into an electrical discharge machine Sodick $\mathrm { V Z 5 0 0 L }$ for the manufacturing process. An aluminum plate of length $1 5 0 ~ \mathrm { m m }$ ,width $2 5 0 ~ \mathrm { m m }$ and thickness $1 \mathrm { m m }$ is chosen as the workpiece. The corresponding cantilevers are cut from the workpiece as per the AutoCAD design fed into the machine by using electric sparks.

The piezoelectric patch made of PZT 5H of dimensions as given in Figure 2 was purchased from Sparkler Ceramics, Pune. The fabricated PVEH in different geometries is shown in Figure 3.

sections.heading: 4.2.2 Experimental setup
sections.text:
The piezoelectric strip made up of PZT 5H is attached to the aluminum base near the fixed end so that it experiences maximum strain. Epofine 138 and Finehard 998 are the adhesives used to make this contact. The piezo strip is attached on the top surface of aluminum at a distance of $1 0 \ \mathrm { m m }$ from the fixed end. For tip excitation (Raju et al., 2015), a permanent magnet is placed at the tip of the aluminum cantilever, as shown in Figure 4. The electromagnetic coil is placed at a fixed distance from the permanent magnet. The distance between the magnets determines the force which is applied across the cantilever beam, as in equation (21). sections.heading: 4.3 Experimental results
sections.text:
The change in resonant frequency with respect to increase in aluminum beam length is analyzed using simulation, experiment and mathematical modeling and is shown in Figure 5. From the mathematical model, the length is inversely proportional to the frequency. This is evident from Figure 5. The output voltage generated for different beam lengths of the harvester is plotted in Figure 6. The magnitude of the voltage generated from the cantilever increases with an increase in the length of the cantilever. It is shown that longer cantilevers will generate a higher voltage at the lower resonant frequency. The harmonic response of three different shaped harvesters is plotted in Figure 7. The maximum average piezoelectric output power is measured for a wide range of electrical loads and is plotted in Figure 8. The resistance range from $1 0 0 \Omega$ to $1 0 ~ \mathrm { { \cal M } \Omega }$ is considered for the analysis. According to the maximum power transfer theorem, maximum power is generated when there is a good impedance matching. Despite the increase in resonant frequency shown by the trapezoidal, the ample increment in potential nullifies the effect of slight increment in resonant frequency. The performance comparison of the rectangular, triangular and trapezoidal cantilever is given in Table V. From Table V, it is inferred that the trapezoidal cantilever shows better performance in terms of the output power. The analytical, simulated and experimental results are close in agreement.

sections.heading: 5 Power conditioning circuitry
sections.text:
The generated AC voltage (Figure 9) is fed into a power conditioning circuitry (Figure 10) for evaluating the performance of the trapezoidal PVEH. The power conditioning circuitry consists of two stages: the rectification stage and the regulation stage. The rectification stage is made of two diodes instead of four diodes. The Schottky diode IN 5818 is chosen, as it has a low forward voltage drop of $1 5 0 – 4 5 0 \mathrm { ~ m V } _ { ; }$ ,which leads to very fast switching action and hence to the achievement of improved efficiency. It also consists of two capacitors. ![](images/95450d18d862f5389121657ecde42dd18311bf5ed78619817bc0a58cfd7997f1.jpg) Figure 9 DSO (050C5) output of trapezoidal PVEH ![](images/2abde90e58a977a327d36e66a6460ccf8e4dd05e8c9d6517bc9826206d43ee03.jpg) Figure 10 Power conditioning circuit Table V Performance comparison

It rectifies the half cycle, and the half of the rectified output is stored in $\mathrm { C } _ { 1 }$ During the negative half cycle, the diode $\mathbf { D } _ { 2 }$ conducts, as it is reverse-biased, and the full rectified output is stored in $\mathrm { C } _ { 2 }$ The LT1761 micro power regulator is used because of its low noise and low dropout characteristics. It is capable of operating over an input voltage from 1.8 to $2 0 \mathrm { V }$ and can supply $1 0 0 \mathrm { m A }$ of output current with a dropout voltage of $3 0 0 \mathrm { m V }$ . The harvested AC voltage $6 6 . 1 3 \mathrm { ~ V ~ }$ (Figure 9) from the proposed trapezoidal cantilever is fed into the power conditioning circuit. The rectified voltage of $2 4 \mathrm { V }$ [Figure 11(a)] is regulated to $3 . 3 \mathrm { V }$ [Figure 11(b)]. As the current output is in terms of micro-Amperes, the regulated DC voltage is used to charge a Li-ion battery GP1S1P-370105. The initial charging is done for several hours. The stored charge is used to turn on C-mote (Chiu et al., 2012). The C-mote is a wireless sensor (WSN) designed with a robust radio frequency front end and highly flexible power management system. The overall experimental setup and the interfacing circuitry are shown in Figure 12. ![](images/87ce6100fa95eca037fbd75d57833ebb26ebd54617db701d04e0cc15acb62485.jpg) Figure 12 Overall experimental setup with power conditioning circuit as a power source to WSN (C-mote)

sections.heading: 6. Conclusion
sections.text: This paper focuses on the design and fabrication of a low-frequency PVEH with an integrated powerconditioning circuit, which consists of rectification and regulation unit. The effect of geometry on the performance of PVEH is analyzed by comparing three different cantilevers. The simulation results are compared with experimental and analytical results. They are found in close agreement. The maximized stress in the trapezoidal cantilever due to the improved strain concentration near the fixed end compared to rectangular and trapezoidal cantilevers leads to improved voltage generation. The generated voltage can be used as a source to power up WSN with the integration of power conditioning circuitry. Furthermore, the power extracted can be maximized by replacing the voltage doubler circuit with advanced power conditioning circuit. The proposed trapezoidal cantilever can be further optimized to improve the conversion efficiency. Further research will be conducted to improve the harvested energy by introducing cavities in the trapezoidal aluminum beam.
